title: Design Dropbox (File Sync)
summary: Keep files in sync even when Wi-Fi drops or two laptops edit at once. Use presigned chunked uploads, content-hash deduplication, a change log per namespace, conflict-safe commits and sharing ACLs.
body:
## Practice first

Design a file storage and sync service. Users upload files from any device, download them anywhere, share files or folders with other people, and see changes made on one laptop appear on their other devices automatically.

Take 10 minutes to list the requirements and entities, write the upload and sync endpoints, and draw a baseline. Choose the deep dives you would lead, then compare your decisions with the walkthrough. You are practicing how to explain a design, not how to reproduce this one.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Upload and download files** of any size up to a limit (say 50 GB) from any device.
2. **Share** a file or folder with other users, as viewer or editor.
3. **Sync automatically:** a change made on one device appears on the user's other devices (and collaborators' devices) without a manual refresh.

Out of scope: real-time collaborative editing inside a document, full-text search over file contents, version history UI beyond keeping the previous revision, billing and quotas UI, and public anonymous links (mention them, but do not design them).

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** 500 million registered users, 100 million daily active, about 1 billion file changes per day.
- **Durability:** an acknowledged upload must never be lost. This is the property users judge the product on; target the eleven-nines object durability that managed object stores advertise and never acknowledge before the bytes and metadata commit are durable.
- **Consistency per operation:** metadata commits for a single file must be linearizable (two devices cannot both "win" silently); sync propagation to other devices can be eventually consistent with a target of a few seconds. Sharing revocation should take effect within seconds.
- **Large-file behaviour:** uploads of multi-gigabyte files must survive flaky networks by resuming, not restarting, and should transfer only the bytes that changed.
- **Availability:** 99.9% or better for download and sync reads; uploads can briefly queue on the client during an outage because the client already holds the bytes locally.

## Back-of-the-envelope

Only estimates that change the design:

- **Bandwidth through app servers:** if 1B changes/day average 1 MB of new bytes, that is 1 PB/day ≈ 11.6 GB/s average, perhaps 35 GB/s at peak. Pushing that through stateless API servers would need hundreds of NICs doing nothing but copying. Decision: **bytes go directly between the client and object storage via presigned URLs**; app servers only handle metadata.
- **Metadata write rate:** 1B changes / 86,400 s ≈ 11,600 commits/s average, ~35,000/s peak. Too much for one relational primary but easy when **sharded by namespace** (a user's root or a shared folder), because almost every transaction touches one namespace.
- **Chunking:** with 4 MB chunks, a 10 GB file is 2,500 chunks. Retrying a failed 10 GB single PUT on a mobile network almost never completes; retrying one 4 MB chunk costs seconds. Decision: **chunked, resumable uploads**.
- **Dedup value:** content-addressed chunks (keyed by SHA-256) mean a re-uploaded or slightly edited file sends only new chunks. Even a 20% dedup ratio at 1 PB/day saves 200 TB/day of transfer and storage.
- **Sync fan-out:** 100M DAU with ~2 devices each is ~200M mostly idle connections. Decision: **long-poll or a lightweight push channel that says "something changed", then the client pulls**, rather than pushing full payloads.

## Core entities

- **File:** id, namespace, path/parent, current revision, size, deleted flag.
- **FileRevision:** an immutable version: ordered list of chunk hashes, size, author device, created time.
- **Chunk:** content hash (SHA-256) → object-store key, size, reference count.
- **Namespace:** a user's root or a shared folder; the unit of sharding, sync cursors and permissions.
- **ShareGrant (ACL):** namespace or file, grantee, role.
- **ChangeLogEntry:** monotonically increasing sequence number per namespace, the file and revision it points to.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    NAMESPACE ||--o{ FILE : contains
    NAMESPACE ||--o{ CHANGE_LOG : orders
    NAMESPACE ||--o{ SHARE_GRANT : grants
    FILE ||--o{ FILE_REVISION : versions
    FILE_REVISION }o--o{ CHUNK : references
    FILE {
        string file_id PK
        string namespace_id
        string path
        string current_rev
    }
    FILE_REVISION {
        string rev_id PK
        string chunk_hashes
        int size
    }
    CHANGE_LOG {
        string namespace_id PK
        int seq PK
        string file_id
    }
```

Think of a file as an ordered chunk list with metadata attached. Each chunk is immutable and addressed by its content hash, so it can be cached, deduplicated and replicated without changing the file's meaning.

## API

```http
POST /v1/files/uploads
Authorization: Bearer <token>
{ "namespaceId": "ns_42", "path": "/docs/plan.pdf", "size": 52428800,
  "chunkHashes": ["sha256:ab12...", "sha256:cd34...", "..."], "baseRev": "rev_17" }

200 OK
{ "uploadId": "up_9", "missingChunks": [
    { "hash": "sha256:cd34...", "putUrl": "https://blob.example.com/...signed...", "expiresAt": "..." } ] }
```

```http
POST /v1/files/uploads/{uploadId}/commit
Authorization: Bearer <token>
Idempotency-Key: 7a1e...
200 OK  { "fileId": "f_1", "rev": "rev_18", "seq": 90211 }
409 Conflict  { "currentRev": "rev_18", "reason": "baseRev is stale" }
```

```http
GET /v1/files/{fileId}/download?rev=rev_18
200 OK { "chunks": [ { "hash": "sha256:ab12...", "getUrl": "https://cdn.example.com/...signed..." } ] }

GET /v1/sync/changes?namespaceId=ns_42&cursor=90180&wait=60
200 OK { "entries": [ { "seq": 90211, "fileId": "f_1", "rev": "rev_18", "op": "update" } ],
         "cursor": "90211", "hasMore": false }

POST /v1/shares
{ "target": "ns_77", "grantee": "user_5", "role": "editor" }
```

Every call is authenticated; the user identity comes from the token. Presigned URLs are short-lived (minutes), scoped to one object and one method. The changes endpoint is cursor-paginated by sequence number and doubles as a long poll when `wait` is set.

## High-level design

**Requirement 1, upload and download.** The client splits the file into 4 MB chunks and hashes each. It asks the Metadata service which hashes are missing; the service answers with presigned PUT URLs for only those. The client uploads chunks directly to the object store, then calls commit. Commit verifies that every referenced chunk exists, then in a single transaction on the namespace's shard creates the new revision, moves the file's `current_rev` pointer and appends a change-log entry. Download is the reverse: metadata returns the chunk list with presigned GET URLs, ideally served through a CDN.

**Requirement 2, share.** A share creates a `ShareGrant` and mounts the shared namespace into the grantee's tree. Every metadata call checks the caller's grants for the namespace; presigned URLs are only minted after that check, so the blob store never needs to know about users.

**Requirement 3, sync.** Each device keeps a cursor per namespace it can see. It long-polls the Notification service; when any of its namespaces advance, the poll returns and the client calls `GET /sync/changes` from its cursor, downloads the missing chunks, and applies them locally.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Desktop or mobile client"] --> GW["API gateway (auth)"]
    GW --> MS["Metadata service"]
    GW --> NS["Notification service (long poll)"]
    MS --> MDB[("Metadata DB, sharded by namespace")]
    MS -->|"presign"| OS[("Object store: chunks")]
    C -->|"PUT and GET chunks"| OS
    OS --> CDN["CDN"]
    CDN --> C
    MS --> CL[["Change log stream"]]
    CL --> NS
```

Walk an edit: a user saves `plan.pdf` on a laptop. The client re-chunks the file and finds that 2 of 13 chunks changed. It requests an upload; metadata replies that only those 2 hashes are missing, with signed URLs. The client PUTs 8 MB to the object store, then commits with `baseRev=rev_17`. The shard transaction succeeds, writing `rev_18` and change-log `seq 90211`, and the commit is published to the change stream. The user's phone, long-polling, wakes, pulls changes after cursor 90180, sees `rev_18`, and downloads the 2 new chunks from the CDN.

## Deep dives

### 1. Large files and flaky networks (resumable, delta uploads)

**Bad: single PUT through the API server.** It doubles bandwidth cost, ties up server memory, hits request-size limits, and any disconnect restarts the whole file.

**Good: presigned direct upload of the whole file, or the store's native multipart upload.** Bytes bypass app servers and multipart lets the client retry individual parts. But a one-byte edit still re-uploads the entire file, and nothing is shared between users who store the same content.

**Great: client-side content-defined or fixed chunking with hash-addressed chunks.** The chunk's SHA-256 is its storage key, so uploading is naturally idempotent and resumable: after a crash, the client re-asks which hashes are missing and continues. Edits upload only new chunks. Fixed 4 MB boundaries are simple; content-defined chunking (rolling hash boundaries) keeps boundaries stable when bytes are inserted near the start of a file, improving delta efficiency at the cost of CPU.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as Metadata service
    participant O as Object store
    C->>C: chunk file, SHA-256 each chunk
    C->>M: start upload (hash list, baseRev)
    M-->>C: missing hashes + presigned PUT URLs
    C->>O: PUT chunk cd34 (retry on failure)
    O-->>C: 200
    C->>M: commit (uploadId, Idempotency-Key)
    M->>O: verify chunks exist
    M->>M: txn: new revision, move pointer, append change log
    M-->>C: rev_18, seq 90211
```

The commit step is the only point where the file becomes visible, so a half-finished upload is invisible garbage rather than a corrupt file. Two safety details: the server must verify the hash of what was stored (otherwise a malicious client can claim a hash it did not upload and poison dedup), and cross-user dedup can leak "this file exists" signals, so many providers dedupe only within an account or verify proof of possession. Orphaned chunks from abandoned uploads are reclaimed by a reference-count or mark-and-sweep garbage collector after a grace period.

### 2. Sync: how devices learn about changes (freshness at scale)

**Bad: clients poll the full file tree every 30 seconds.** 200M devices listing trees is wasted work and still feels slow.

**Good: periodic polling of a per-namespace change log with a cursor.** Each namespace has a monotonically increasing sequence assigned inside the commit transaction. Clients ask "what changed after seq N?" which is a cheap index range scan, and resume exactly where they left off after being offline for a week.

**Great: change log plus long-poll (or WebSocket/SSE) notifications.** The device holds one long-poll per account to a Notification service that subscribes to the change stream. The notification carries no data, only "namespace X advanced"; the client then pulls from the change log. This keeps the push channel stateless and cheap and keeps the change log as the single source of truth. If a notification is dropped, the next poll timeout (say 60 s) or reconnect catches up, so the system is eventually consistent with a bounded delay.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Phone
    participant N as Notification service
    participant K as Change stream
    participant M as Metadata service
    P->>N: long poll (namespaces and cursors)
    K-->>N: ns_42 advanced to 90211
    N-->>P: ns_42 changed
    P->>M: GET changes after 90180
    M-->>P: entries, new cursor 90211
    P->>P: download new chunks, apply locally
```

A notification only says "check for changes"; pulling from the cursor is how the device learns what changed. If log compaction has removed that cursor's history, return a "reset" so the client performs one full listing and starts fresh.

### 3. Conflicts between devices (linearizable commits)

Picture two laptops editing the same file offline. When both reconnect, each wants to commit a different version based on the same starting revision.

**Bad: last writer wins by timestamp.** Clock skew picks an arbitrary winner and silently discards someone's work.

**Good: optimistic concurrency on the revision pointer.** Commit includes `baseRev`; the transaction does `UPDATE file SET current_rev = :new WHERE file_id = :id AND current_rev = :baseRev`. Zero rows updated means someone else committed first; return 409.

**Great: optimistic concurrency plus a conflicted copy.** On 409 the losing client keeps its bytes (they are already uploaded as chunks), commits them as a sibling file such as `plan (Laptop's conflicted copy).pdf`, and the user resolves it. Nothing is lost, the server stays simple, and the rule is predictable. Renames and moves are handled the same way: they are metadata commits guarded by the parent's revision, and moving across namespaces is a copy-then-delete because two shards cannot share one local transaction.

### 4. Metadata scale and sharding (throughput and isolation)

At ~35,000 commits/s, shard the metadata store by `namespace_id`. One commit touches one file, its revision, and one change-log row, all in the same namespace, so it is a single-shard ACID transaction and the per-namespace sequence can come from that shard. A relational database (sharded MySQL or Postgres) or a distributed SQL store both fit. Hot namespaces (a company-wide shared folder) are the main risk: rate-limit per namespace and split very large orgs into multiple namespaces. The change-log table is append-only and can be trimmed after, say, 30 days, with older cursors forced to a full resync.

### 5. Sharing and access control (security)

Store grants as rows keyed by `(namespace_id, grantee)` and check them on every metadata call, caching per-user permission sets for a few seconds. Folder-level grants inherit downward by namespace, which avoids per-file ACL explosions. Revocation deletes the grant and invalidates the cache; because blob access is only via presigned URLs with short expiry (for example 5 minutes), the worst case after revocation is one already-issued URL living out its TTL. Never make object keys guessable or the bucket public, and do not embed user ids in chunk keys, since chunks are shared by hash.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** a working upload/download path that keeps bytes off app servers, a metadata store separate from blob storage, and some way for other devices to learn about changes.
- **Senior:** drives chunking with content hashes for resumability and deltas, a per-namespace change log with cursors, long-poll notifications as hints, optimistic concurrency for conflicts, and a sharding key justified by transaction boundaries.
- **Staff:** reasons about dedup security (proof of possession, existence leaks), chunk garbage collection, change-log compaction and client resync, hot shared namespaces, cross-region durability, and the client as half of the distributed system (local state database, crash recovery, bandwidth throttling).

## Common mistakes

- Streaming file bytes through the API servers.
- Making the file visible before all chunks are uploaded, so other devices download a partial file.
- Using timestamps for conflict resolution.
- Pushing full file contents through WebSockets to every device.
- Trusting the client's claimed chunk hash without server verification.
- Sharding metadata by `file_id`, which turns every folder listing and change-log read into a scatter-gather.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] Bytes flow client ↔ object store directly via short-lived presigned URLs.
- [ ] Uploads are chunked, resumable and idempotent, with a single commit that makes them visible.
- [ ] Each device can catch up from an arbitrary offline period using a cursor.
- [ ] Concurrent edits are detected with a revision check and resolved without data loss.
- [ ] The shard key keeps every commit within one shard.
- [ ] Revocation latency is bounded and you can state the bound.
- [ ] Orphaned chunks are garbage-collected.

keyTakeaways: Send file bytes straight between the client and object storage with short-lived presigned URLs. Keep app servers focused on metadata.
Hash-addressed chunks let uploads resume safely, retry idempotently and transfer only changed chunks. One metadata commit makes the new revision visible.
Sync from a per-namespace change log using cursors. Long-poll notifications are hints to pull; the log is the source of truth.
Check the revision pointer with optimistic concurrency to catch competing edits. Save a conflicted copy so neither version disappears.
Shard metadata by namespace to keep each commit, its change-log entry and folder listings on one shard.
